content.p: Jussie Smollett, an actor who played Jamal Lyon on the Fox drama "Empire," told Chicago police in January 2019 that two masked men had attacked him in the early morning, shouted racial and homophobic slurs, and put a rope around his neck. Within weeks the case had turned into a criminal prosecution of Smollett himself. It ended in a 2021 jury verdict, a 2022 jail sentence, and a 2024 ruling by the Illinois Supreme Court that threw out the conviction. The court did not decide whether he was innocent, and Smollett has repeatedly denied staging the attack.

Smollett went to the Chicago Police Department on 29 January 2019 and described an assault that he said happened as he walked out for food at about 2 a.m. after returning from New York. He said the attackers hurled racist and homophobic slurs, beat him, doused him with a substance he believed was bleach, and looped a noose around his neck in the Streeterville neighborhood. Police later said he told detectives that the attackers had yelled "MAGA country," a reference to the slogan of Donald Trump's presidential campaign. The Salt Lake Tribune reported that he said the attackers poured an "unknown substance" on him.

The case drew national attention almost at once. Police said they were treating the report as a possible hate crime and released images from a surveillance camera near the scene. On 31 January the president said from the Oval Office that the attack was "horrible." Smollett's family said in a statement that the attack was "a racial and homophobic hate crime," and Smollett said at the time that he had been "100% factual and consistent on every level."
content.h2: Doubts and a change of direction
content.p: The investigation then moved in a different direction. Smollett declined to hand over his phone, saying it held private pictures and videos. He gave detectives a partial, redacted list of call records on 11 February, thirteen days after the reported attack. On 14 February, Chicago police said they had identified two persons of interest, two Nigerian brothers; NBC News reported that at least one of them had worked on "Empire." The police released the brothers on the night of 15 February without charging them, and by 16 February a police source was telling NBC News that the probe had shifted to whether Smollett had paid the two men to stage an assault.

Superintendent Eddie Johnson had already said on 1 February that the allegations, as described to police, were "horrendous, horrible, and quite frankly cowardly." Chicago police spokesman Guglielmi said on 17 February that investigators needed to speak again with the man who had made the report. Smollett's lawyers said he would not meet detectives that day and denied that he was complicit.
content.h2: A charge, an indictment and a sudden dismissal
content.p: The Cook County State's Attorney charged Smollett on 20 February 2019 with a single count of disorderly conduct, accusing him of filing a false police report. NBC News later reported that, because of the allegations, his role on "Empire" had been cut from the final episodes of the show's fifth season. In early March a grand jury returned a 16-count indictment that, according to the Salt Lake Tribune, accused him of making a false report about an offense.

Less than three weeks after the indictment, the State's Attorney's Office dropped every charge. Under the deal, Smollett forfeited a $10,000 bond to the city and performed community service, and prosecutors agreed to expunge the record. The office said the outcome was "a just disposition and appropriate resolution to this case." Chicago's police leadership and former mayor Rahm Emanuel criticized the decision. Emanuel called it a "whitewash of justice" that gave special treatment to a celebrity. State's Attorney Kim Foxx faced sharp criticism over the decision.
content.h2: A special prosecutor and a second case
content.p: In August 2019 a judge appointed former U.S. Attorney Dan Webb as special prosecutor after a retired judge asked for a special prosecutor, and a judge found that the state's attorney had not followed procedure when she stepped aside from the case. Webb said he would use a special grand jury and was "starting this thing fresh." He later sought a new six-count indictment, and a grand jury agreed to charge Smollett with making four separate false reports to Chicago police officers.

Webb's office also examined how the original deal had been reached. In a summary report unsealed in December 2021, the special prosecutor said the office could not explain why it had moved to drop the first charges 19 days after the indictment, and the report called this a "major failure of operations." Webb's team reported that it found no evidence of crime by Foxx or anyone else in the office. Webb said the office had cited 5,700 similar cases, but the team could not find one resolved the same way. Foxx's legal counsel called the report "deeply flawed" and said the statements in question could be attributed to bad information or a "failed recollection."

At the trial in December 2021, the jury heard testimony from the two brothers, who said Smollett had paid them to carry out the attack. Prosecutors said Smollett had told the men which slurs to shout and to yell about "MAGA Country," and the brothers testified that he had paid them $3,500. Smollett testified that he had not recognised the men and that the attack was real. He also said he had become friends with Abimbola Osundairo during filming, and his lawyers argued that the brothers had taken advantage of him and that the check was for personal training.

The jury found him guilty on five of six counts of felony disorderly conduct. Judge James Linn rejected a defence motion to overturn the verdict on legal grounds and said he believed Smollett had received a fair trial. In March 2022, the judge ordered 150 days in county jail and 30 months of felony probation, and denied a request to suspend the sentence. Prosecutors asked for "an appropriate amount of prison time," and the defence asked for community service. Chicago's police superintendent, David Brown, whose statement was read aloud in court, said that Smollett's false report had harmed "actual victims" of hate crimes and asked that the city be compensated. Smollett shouted "I am innocent" as deputies led him out of the courtroom.

The sentence also included a $25,000 fine and restitution to the city. The figures differ: NBC Chicago reported an order of more than $120,000, while WBEZ reported that the special prosecutor had asked for $130,000, and Webb said the false reports had cost the city $130,000 in overtime pay.

Smollett was released from custody pending appeal. An Illinois appeals court upheld the conviction in a 2-1 ruling. The majority rejected the argument that the 2019 agreement with the State's Attorney's Office barred a second prosecution. A dissenting judge read the agreement as a complete resolution of the matter, not a temporary one.

On 21 November 2024, the Illinois Supreme Court ruled 5-0, with Chief Justice Mary Jane Theis and Justice Joy Cunningham abstaining, that the 2019 dismissal was a binding non-prosecution agreement. The court held that "a second prosecution under these circumstances is a due process violation," and reversed the conviction. Justice Elizabeth Rochford wrote the opinion. She acknowledged that the original resolution had been criticized as unjust, but wrote that "what would be more unjust than the resolution of any one criminal case would be a holding from this court that the State was not bound to honor agreements upon which people have detrimentally relied."

Webb said he was disappointed by the ruling and that Illinois case law did not preclude a new prosecution after a dismissal without prejudice. He said the ruling "has nothing to do with Mr. Smollett's innocence," and that the court had not found error in the trial evidence. Smollett's lawyer, Nenye Uche, called the case "a vindictive persecution" and said the ruling restored the rule of law. Smollett's team has said he is innocent.

The Supreme Court did not decide whether the attack happened as Smollett described it. Its ruling rested on the 2019 agreement. Webb said the court had not found error with the "overwhelming evidence" presented at trial, which had led the jury to find him guilty of five counts of felony disorderly conduct. Smollett's position, that the attack was real and that he was the victim, has not changed.

Several points remain contested. The brothers' names are given differently by different outlets. The restitution figure differs between accounts. Whether the original dismissal was a proper exercise of prosecutorial discretion is also disputed: Webb's report called it an operational failure, while Foxx's counsel said the report was flawed and that the office had not been involved after she stepped aside.
